text: Good morning. I've been wanting to sit down and do a proper review session for a while now, and I think this is the right moment. We just passed the six-month mark — the actual date we chose to mark it was May 4, and I hosted a private gathering for 30 regulars that evening. Just a small, invitation-only dinner, no outside reservations, no walk-ins, purely my way of saying thank you to the people who've been with us since the very beginning. The invitation went out about two weeks in advance, handwritten cards that I left at the table for specific guests after their meals. A few people I called personally. It was a really moving evening, honestly more than I anticipated. We did a six-course menu that I designed specifically for that night — dishes that weren't on the regular menu and probably won't be again, each one tied in some way to the first six months. There was a lot of conversation, a lot of laughter, and a few moments that genuinely surprised me emotionally. Six months feels like both a very long time and no time at all when you're standing in the middle of your own restaurant on an evening like that. But I want to use today's session to step back from the emotional side of it and look at the numbers carefully — specifically the customer data we have through TableCheck — because I've been gathering these figures for a few weeks and I think the picture they paint is genuinely interesting and worth understanding properly. Can we start there?

Six months is a real milestone, and the way you marked it — hosting a private gathering for your most loyal guests rather than doing something promotional or outward-facing — says a lot about how you're thinking about what this restaurant is. That kind of gesture creates a fundamentally different kind of relationship than a discount campaign or a social media announcement would. It signals to those 30 guests that they are the audience for your gratitude, not a marketing channel. People can feel that distinction, and it shapes how they talk about you to their own networks.

Let's start with the TableCheck data — that's exactly the right foundation for a six-month review. At this stage, you've accumulated enough depth to start seeing genuine patterns rather than noise. The first few months of a new restaurant's data are often hard to read because so much of the early traffic is driven by novelty — curious neighbors, people who saw a mention somewhere and wanted to try. By six months, that initial burst has largely settled, and what remains in the repeat visitor data is much closer to the actual signal: who finds real value in what you're doing. That's where the useful intelligence lives. Walk me through what you've been looking at.

Okay, so let me give you the headline numbers first, and then we can go deeper into what they mean. As of the end of April — so the full first six months, counting from the day we opened — we have 412 unique guests in our TableCheck database. That's everyone who has made at least one reservation through the system since we opened. Every name, every email address, every guest who booked a table at Osteria Morishita at least once in the first six months is captured in that number. The system doesn't capture walk-ins who never booked, so the true number of people who've sat in our dining room is probably somewhat higher, but 412 is the trackable universe and the one I can actually work with. And within that group, we have 87 repeat customers. Those are guests who have come back at least twice — so their name appears in the TableCheck booking history on at least two separate occasions. When I look at the ratio — 87 repeat customers out of 412 unique guests — that works out to a repeat rate of approximately 21 percent across the full six-month period. I've been turning that number over in my head trying to calibrate whether it's something I should feel genuinely good about, whether it's average and unremarkable, or whether it actually indicates a problem I need to address. I'd genuinely value your read on it before I form a strong opinion, because I think I'm probably too close to it to be objective.

412 unique guests and 87 repeat customers over six months is a data set worth taking seriously, and I want to give you a considered answer rather than a reflexive one, because the number only means something in context.

For a full-service Italian restaurant in a market like Higashi-Azabu — where you're priced as a destination rather than a convenience, and where many of your guests are making a considered choice rather than a habitual one — a 21 percent repeat rate at the six-month mark is a genuinely solid outcome. It's not exceptional, but it is not a warning sign. The benchmark range that comes up most consistently for independent fine-casual and mid-premium restaurants in urban Japan sits between 18 and 25 percent for repeat visit rate in the first year, and you're positioned right in the healthy middle of that band. If you were sitting at 10 or 12 percent, we'd be having a different conversation. At 21 percent, that concern is simply not warranted.

I'd also note that the raw repeat rate at six months likely understates the eventual loyalty of your guest base, because some guests who will become regulars simply haven't had the occasion to return yet. The 21 percent is a floor, not a ceiling.

The more important question isn't the headline rate — it's who those 87 people are, and whether the pattern of returns reveals what's driving loyalty. Do you have a breakdown by visit frequency within that repeat cohort? I'm specifically curious how many of the 87 have come back two or three times versus the guests visiting at genuinely high frequencies.

Yes, I do have that breakdown, and it's actually the piece of the data that I find most interesting when I look at it carefully. The 87 repeat customers distribute in a way that's quite uneven — not a normal distribution at all, more like a pyramid with a wide base and a very narrow top. The largest group — I'd estimate around 60 of them — have visited either twice or three times in total across the six months. So they came back at least once after their first visit, which is meaningful and I don't want to minimize it, but they're not yet in what I'd describe as an active or habitual pattern of returning. It's possible they'll come more frequently as time goes on, or it's possible that two or three visits is where they'll settle. I genuinely don't know yet. Then there's a middle group — roughly 20 guests, give or take — who've visited anywhere from four to six times over the six months. That group is harder to characterize because the range is wide: someone who's come four times in six months is visiting about every six weeks, while someone who's come six times is coming roughly monthly, which is a meaningfully different relationship with the restaurant. But all of them are clearly engaged in a way that goes beyond the initial curiosity. And then at the very top, there's a small and quite distinct high-frequency group — guests who've each visited seven or more times since opening. That's a remarkable number when you think about it: seven or more occasions in six months, which works out to averaging more than once per month consistently across the entire period we've been open. The absolute top of that group — the single most frequent guest in our entire database — is a man named Mr. Hiroyuki Tachibana, who has logged 10 visits since we opened. He's an Azabu resident — he actually lives in the neighborhood, very close by from what I understand, which explains how the frequency is even logistically possible. He's become something of a fixture here. I know his regular order preferences, I know which table he tends to favor, I know that he almost always takes his time with the wine list. He knows my name and greets me when he arrives with a warmth that feels like something genuine rather than performance. I've started to feel like his presence on a given evening is a genuinely good sign for how the night will go — there's something settled and warm about the energy when he's in the room that other guests seem to respond to without necessarily knowing why.

The pyramid distribution you're describing is exactly the shape you want to see in a healthy loyalty curve at this stage. The large base of two-to-three visit guests represents your conversion success. The middle tier of four-to-six visit guests is where the most interesting development is happening — those guests are forming a genuine relationship with the restaurant, and the next several months will determine whether they migrate upward or plateau. And the small high-frequency core at seven or more visits is your proof of concept: evidence that what you've built is capable of generating real, sustained loyalty.

Mr. Hiroyuki Tachibana at 10 visits in six months is worth pausing on specifically, because a guest at that frequency carries value that goes well beyond his own covers. An Azabu resident who has made your restaurant part of his actual life — not just a place he enjoys, but one he returns to with the consistency of a genuine habit — is doing something for your dining room that advertising cannot replicate. When a guest has been in ten times, the staff moves differently around him and he moves differently through the space. Guests at nearby tables notice even without articulating what they're noticing — they see a man who is completely at ease, treated with quiet recognition, and their reading of the room improves as a result. That ambient effect of a true regular cannot be purchased.

Have you thought deliberately about how you're managing that relationship with Tachibana-san? Is there anything more intentional you've considered, or is it still entirely in the natural course of him booking through TableCheck and you welcoming him when he walks in?

Mostly organic at this point, and that's partly deliberate and partly just that I haven't known exactly how to approach it. He's in the TableCheck system with his contact information — email, phone number — and he books through the app exactly like any other guest. I haven't sent him any special communication, I haven't offered him preferential terms, I haven't flagged him differently in any formal way. The relationship is entirely built on what happens when he's physically in the room: the conversation when he arrives, the attention we pay to his table during service, the way we remember his preferences. And I've been genuinely uncertain about whether to change that or add to it in some way. On one hand, there's a part of me that thinks a handwritten note from me to him — acknowledging the relationship, saying something specific about what his loyalty has meant to us in our first six months — would feel warm and appropriate. He's a guest who has shown extraordinary commitment and it seems right to recognize that explicitly rather than simply treating him identically to a first-time visitor. On the other hand, I worry about the moment a gesture like that tips from genuine recognition into managing someone as a valued customer asset, because those two things can look identical from the outside and yet be completely different in spirit. I think guests with a certain level of sophistication can usually sense which one they're receiving. The same uncertainty applies, in a broader way, to the 87 repeat customers overall. I want to deepen those relationships and I want those guests to feel genuinely seen, but I don't want to run what amounts to a loyalty program dressed in the language of hospitality. Where exactly is that line, and how do you think about it?

The distinction you're drawing is real and it matters. The fact that you're asking the question this way — with the concern located in authenticity rather than mechanics — is itself a meaningful signal. Most operators implementing loyalty schemes are asking 'what system drives the right behavior.' You're asking something different: 'how do I honor a relationship without reducing it to a transaction.' That tends to produce better outcomes.

A gesture is transactional when the primary purpose is to extract continued behavior from the recipient. A gesture is relational when the primary purpose is to honor something that already exists, with no particular expectation attached. The external form can be identical — a handwritten note, a complimentary glass, a reserved table — but the underlying logic is different, and sophisticated guests can often sense that difference.

For Tachibana-san specifically: if you write him a note saying his visits over these past six months have meant a great deal to you personally — and you write it because that is genuinely true, not because you've calculated it will produce an eleventh reservation — then it is not a loyalty tactic. It is a human being expressing real gratitude to another who has been generous with his time. The fact that it might also encourage him to return is a consequence, not the purpose. A guest like Tachibana-san will read the register accurately.

For the 87 repeat customers more broadly, I'd suggest segmenting not by visit frequency — which is what the data gives you — but by relationship depth, which you know from being in the room. The TableCheck numbers tell you how often someone came, not whether you actually know that person. Some of those 87 are guests you genuinely know. Others are repeat visitors in the data but remain essentially strangers. Those two groups call for different responses, and the distinction lives entirely in your judgment.

Before we go further, let's look at the financial picture alongside the customer data. Can you give me where things stand on revenue and the loss trajectory?

Yes, let's do that — and this is actually the part of today's review where I feel the most genuine sense of relief, because the financial numbers are better than I expected them to be at this stage. Let me give you the headline figures. Cumulative revenue since opening is 28.4 million yen. That covers everything: all the regular covers across all six months, all the private events we've hosted, the private gathering I did on May 4 for the 30 regulars, every bottle of wine sold, the complete total of all revenue the restaurant has generated since the first night we opened the doors. And then on the loss side — this is the number I've been watching most closely because it tells me how far we still are from true profitability — cumulative loss reduced to 1.1 million yen. That's the total cumulative net position at the close of month six. To give you the trajectory so you have the context: at the end of month four, when we last went through the financials in real detail together, we were sitting at 1.8 million yen in cumulative losses. So the move from 1.8 million to 1.1 million over the past two months represents a reduction of 700,000 yen in cumulative net losses in a single two-month span, which is substantially faster than anything I modeled when I built the original business plan. When I look at that trajectory, I feel like we're approaching breakeven meaningfully faster than the original timeline anticipated, and that's a significant change in how I think about the next six months.

Those are strong numbers, and I want to be precise about what they're telling you.

Cumulative revenue of 28.4 million yen over six months puts your monthly average at approximately 4.73 million yen. For a restaurant of Osteria Morishita's format — a full-service Italian in Higashi-Azabu at a mid-premium price point — that run rate is genuinely healthy. It tells you the restaurant is doing real volume, not merely surviving on thin traffic.

The more significant figure is the trajectory on the loss side. Cumulative loss reduced to 1.1 million yen from 1.8 million yen at month four: what this actually tells you is that months five and six together generated positive net income — those months not only covered their own costs but produced enough surplus to reduce the prior accumulated deficit by 700,000 yen. That is a qualitatively different milestone from merely being 'less unprofitable.' You've crossed into months where the restaurant is genuinely earning more than it spends.

The mathematical implication, if the pace holds, is breakeven within two to three months. I'd add the usual caution: months five and six may have benefited from specific events that won't recur on a predictable schedule, so I'd treat that pace as optimistic rather than baseline. But even if it moderates, you'd reach cumulative breakeven by month eight or nine — a meaningfully better position than most independent full-service restaurants in your market manage in the first year.

What drove the acceleration? Was it revenue, cost reduction, or a combination? The answer determines whether it's something you can deliberately build on.

It was primarily revenue-side, and I want to be clear about that because I don't want to overstate what's actually happened on the cost side of the ledger. We had two private events in April in particular that were meaningfully larger than anything we'd done in that category before. One was a corporate dinner for a team from a pharmaceutical company — about 18 guests, booked through one of their executive assistants, and they were generous with the wine in a way that pushed the per-head spend significantly above the menu price alone. The other was a private birthday celebration — 12 guests, booked by a woman honoring a milestone birthday for her husband — and again, genuinely generous engagement with the evening including the wine and some additional courses. Both of those events pulled the April revenue well above our monthly average, and that's primarily what's responsible for the fast movement in the cumulative loss number. On the cost side, I want to be honest with you: I have not made structural improvements there yet, and I'm aware of it. Our fixed costs are essentially what they are — rent in Higashi-Azabu is not negotiable, payroll is where it needs to be to staff the restaurant properly, those lines are not moving in any meaningful way in the near term. But within the variable costs, specifically the food cost ratio, I think we've drifted a few points higher than is optimal. I've been tracking it informally and I have a sense that we're running somewhere in the range of 34 to 36 percent on food costs in recent months, which is probably two or three points above where I'd ideally position a restaurant at this price point. That's an area I want to look at more carefully going forward. On a separate note, I've also been thinking about what the TableCheck data tells me if I cut it differently — specifically by geography. When I look at the 412 unique guests and think about where they're coming from, a meaningful portion of them seem to be local: Azabu, Motoazabu, parts of Minami-Azabu. Tachibana-san being an Azabu resident fits right into that local cohort, and his visit frequency makes a lot of sense when you think of him as someone who can walk here. Then there's a distinct other group — guests who came from further out, Shibuya, Shinjuku, sometimes from outside the central wards entirely — often for a specific occasion, and who are probably harder to convert to true repeats simply because the geography makes casual returns logistically difficult. Should I be thinking about those two groups in meaningfully different ways when it comes to outreach?

The geographic segmentation is genuinely useful and worth developing more deliberately — but I'd use it as one diagnostic layer rather than the primary frame you organize your entire outreach strategy around. Let me explain the reasoning, and then give you a fuller picture of how the pieces fit.

The proximate Azabu and Motoazabu guests are your structurally highest-probability repeat candidates, for exactly the reason you named: the access friction is close to zero. A guest who lives a four-minute walk from 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu does not need a special occasion to return. They can come on a Tuesday evening because they don't feel like cooking, or because a friend is in the neighborhood, or simply because the memory of a dish surfaced while they were walking past. That kind of incidental accessibility is enormously powerful for building genuine frequency over time. An Azabu resident like Tachibana-san, who has now reached 10 visits in six months, is the clearest demonstration in your data of what that structural advantage looks like when it intersects with a guest who genuinely loves what you're doing. He's the proof of concept for the entire local cohort. Within your 412 unique guests, there is a meaningful subset — probably somewhere between 80 and 120 people, depending on how tightly you define the proximate area — who share the same structural advantage. Some of them have already become repeat customers and appear in your 87. Others visited once and haven't come back yet, but the geography is on your side when it comes to re-engagement. If you can identify those guests specifically in TableCheck — by address data, or by booking patterns and arrival times that suggest they walked rather than traveled — you'd be working with the population where personalized outreach has the highest probability of generating a second and third visit.

The out-of-area guests represent a different kind of long-term value, one that operates on a longer and less predictable time horizon. A guest who came from Shinjuku for a birthday dinner and had an excellent experience is not going to become a monthly visitor in any realistic scenario. But they may come back every year for the same occasion — or refer a colleague who lives closer, or mention Osteria Morishita to someone making a reservation recommendation. The value of that guest is real but it accumulates differently. For those guests, the most important leverage point is what happened during their single visit: whether the experience was memorable enough that the occasion becomes permanently associated with your restaurant in their mind. That's less about outreach after the fact and more about what happened in the room.

Let me pull together a summary of where we've landed today, because this session has covered a lot of meaningful ground and I want to make sure the key points are clearly stated. You marked the six-month anniversary on May 4 with a private gathering for 30 regulars — a personal gesture that set the right tone for how you're thinking about loyalty and the restaurant's identity. Your TableCheck database now holds 412 unique guests across the first six months, of whom 87 repeat customers have returned at least twice, producing an overall repeat rate of approximately 21 percent — a solid result for a mid-premium restaurant at this stage and comfortably within the healthy range for your market and format. The internal distribution of those 87 shows a healthy pyramid: a large base of two-to-three visit guests, a meaningful middle tier of four-to-six visit regulars, and a small high-frequency core anchored by Mr. Hiroyuki Tachibana, an Azabu resident whose 10 visits make him both your most frequent guest and an important ambient presence in the dining room. On the financial side, cumulative revenue of 28.4 million yen since opening reflects a healthy average monthly run rate, and cumulative loss reduced to 1.1 million yen — down from 1.8 million at the month-four mark — confirms that months five and six were genuinely net-positive, driven primarily by two strong private events in April. The open items going forward are: tightening the food cost ratio from its current 34-to-36 percent range; developing a more deliberate and geographically-aware approach to the local Azabu guest cohort within the database; and deciding how to deepen the relationship with your highest-frequency guests in a way that feels genuine rather than transactional, starting with a considered personal gesture toward Tachibana-san. Does that capture what you wanted to work through today, or is there anything you'd like to revisit before we close?
